items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-26
items.q: They had Johnny Fisher's band, he's still a failure.

ctx.x: Well now, the bands, they played regular popular tunes. I never heard any numbers that was improvised or worked on. If they played a chorus of different tunes, they may have had a little bit flourishes to it with their own. I don't say they didn't do that, but they were playing ragtime. I played ragtime. And the rhythm wasn't changing until I hit Chicago. Now this is going to be a strange thing and this is why they say the miracle couldn't happen. There was a dance team called, wait a minute, the castles. And at…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-16
items.q: Now Johnny Fisher brought his band to New York. He was a failure.

ctx.x: Pioneer of jazz wins recognition, New Orleans, editor from New Orleans States. It was gratifying to read in your paper on February 27th the article on Nick LaRocca, famous leader of the original Dixieland jazz band. He deserves the honor accorded him and his band by the Jazz Club of England whose leader, Marcus O'Donoghau visited our sea last summer. If Mr. LaRocca accepts this invitation, and I hope he does, I'm sure he will mention some of the other bands that played jazz at that time. Tom Brown, who took his…

I'd like to comment on the dates that she has here to show you she was eaten up, taken in by this communist propaganda. I wish you'd hear this tape recorder. Buddy Bolin, Freddie Kepler, George Pequet left here in 1911. In 1906, by the things that I have in my hand, from Louisiana State Mental Hospital at Jackson, Louisiana, Bolin was incarcerated in there in 1906. He couldn't have played with them. And I've told you when these Negroes came it was 1917. Clarence Williams, he says, left here around 1911 or 13.…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-21
items.q: Then came Johnny Fisher and his ragtime group.

ctx.x: I didn't know it. Because there's many people came to New York that I didn't know. They had a band here that I didn't know here. After the

Creole band, the next band to come to New York City was Lacrosse Harmony Quintet. They opened at the Golden Glades. They stayed with about four weeks. The pianists went with Gellert, Gladys Morley, and Barbara. They never were heard again. This was a white group. I had never known these boys. Then came Con Brown with his reorganized band to New York City, where they tried to arise letters, and the management walked out while they were playing.
